parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Explain, with reference to forces acting on the stone, the shape of the curve in Fig. 2.1.

markscheme_points.text: resultant force decreases (as speed increases/with time) so acceleration decreases (as speed increases/with time)
when air resistance equals the weight the speed/velocity/v becomes constant

hints: Hint 1: Start by listing the two vertical forces on the falling stone and which one stays constant and which one grows as the stone goes faster.
Hint 2: Think about how the difference between those two forces - the resultant force - changes, and what $F = ma$ then says about acceleration and the gradient of the $v$-$t$ graph.
Hint 3: Consider what must happen to the motion when the upward force has grown until it exactly balances the downward force.
parts.proper_answer: As speed increases air resistance (drag) upwards increases. Weight downwards is constant, so resultant force downwards $W - R$ decreases, so acceleration decreases and gradient of $v$-$t$ decreases. When air resistance equals weight, resultant force is zero, acceleration is zero and velocity becomes constant at terminal velocity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **The two forces at play**
A falling stone always has its weight $W = mg$ pulling down. It is essentially constant. Opposing the motion is air resistance $R$ acting up. Drag gets bigger when speed gets bigger, roughly like faster means more air to push aside each second.

Step 2: **Why the curve flattens**
The resultant force down is $$F = W - R$$ At the start $v$ is small, $R$ is small, so $F$ is large and close to $W$. From $F = ma$, acceleration is large, so the $v$-$t$ graph is steep. As $v$ grows, $R$ grows, so $F = W - R$ shrinks. That means $a$ shrinks, so the gradient of the $v$-$t$ graph gets smaller and smaller. That gives the curved shape levelling off.

Step 3: **Reaching constant speed**
Eventually $R$ grows until $$R = W$$ Then $F = 0$, so $a = 0$. With no acceleration velocity cannot increase further. The graph becomes horizontal. This constant speed is terminal velocity.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Use Fig. 2.1 to determine the speed of the stone when the resultant force on it is zero.
hints: Hint 1: Link zero resultant force to acceleration using $F = ma$, then think about what zero acceleration looks like on the $v$-$t$ graph in Fig. 2.1.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot zero acceleration on the graph**
Zero resultant force means $$F = ma = 0$$ so $a = 0$. On a $v$-$t$ graph acceleration is the gradient, so you need the flat, horizontal section where velocity stops increasing.

Step 2: **Read the value**
In Fig. 2.1 the curve levels off at about $36\text{ m s}^{-1}$ from roughly $t = 20\text{ s}$ onwards. That plateau is the terminal speed when resultant force is zero.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Use Fig. 2.1 to calculate the approximate height through which the stone falls between $t = 0$ and $t = 30\text{ s}$.

markscheme_points.text: height given by area under the curve
height = 950 m. Round to two significant figures and award 2 marks for a value in the range 920–980 m and 1 mark for a value in the range 900–910 m or 990–1000 m.

hints: Hint 1: Recall what physical quantity you get when you multiply velocity by time, and what that means for the area under a $v$-$t$ graph.
Hint 2: Work out the distance represented by one small grid square on Fig. 2.1, then think about how to count whole squares plus parts of squares under the curve to $t = 30\text{ s}$.
Hint 3: Combine your square count to get total height fallen and give the result to a sensible 2 significant figures because it is an estimate.
parts.proper_answer: Height is area under $v$-$t$ graph between $t = 0$ and $t = 30\text{ s}$. Area $\approx 950\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Area means distance**
For any motion, small distance $\Delta s = v \Delta t$. Adding them up is exactly the area under the $v$-$t$ graph. So height fallen is $$s = \text{area under curve from 0 to 30 s}$$

Step 2: **Count the squares**
Look at the grid. On the $t$-axis a small square is $0.5\text{ s}$ and on the $v$-axis a small square is $0.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$. So one small square is $$0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25\text{ m}$$ Counting all the small squares under the curve to $30\text{ s}$ gives about 3800 squares. A quicker way is to count large squares and multiply. Either way you get $$s \approx 3800 \times 0.25 \approx 950\text{ m}$$

Step 3: **Give an approximate answer**
Because you are estimating by eye, $900$ to $1000\text{ m}$ is acceptable. A good central value is $$s \approx 9.5 \times 10^2\text{ m}$$ to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: (b)(iv)

markscheme_points.text: curve with negative gradient between t = 0 and t = 20 s
line showing zero acceleration between t = 20 s and t = 30 s

hints: Hint 1: Think about the gradient of Fig. 2.1 at $t = 0$ when speed and air resistance are still zero, and what that tells you about the starting value of $a$.
Hint 2: Describe how the gradient of the $v$-$t$ graph changes between $t = 0$ and about $t = 20\text{ s}$, and what that means for the shape of the $a$-$t$ graph.
Hint 3: Decide what the acceleration must stay at once terminal velocity is reached after about $t = 20\text{ s}$.
parts.proper_answer: Curve starting at $a = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ at $t = 0$, with decreasing negative gradient falling toward zero, reaching $a = 0$ by about $t = 20\text{ s}$ and remaining at zero to $t = 30\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the starting point**
Acceleration is the gradient of $v$ against $t$, $$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$ At $t = 0$, $v = 0$ so air resistance is zero. The only force is weight, so $a = g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Your $a$-$t$ graph must start at $(0, 9.8)$.

Step 2: **Follow the gradient**
In Fig. 2.1 the $v$-$t$ gradient is steepest at the start and gets less steep all the time. So $a$ must fall continuously. The fall is fastest at first then slows, giving a curve with negative gradient that itself flattens - a decay shape.

Step 3: **Finish flat at zero**
Once terminal velocity is reached at about $20\text{ s}$, gradient is zero, so $a = 0$. From $t = 20\text{ s}$ to $30\text{ s}$ draw a horizontal line along the $t$-axis at $a = 0$.

key_concepts: acceleration as rate of change of velocity
vector nature of velocity
hints: Hint 1: Start from $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$ and name the changing vector quantity, not just speed.
parts.proper_answer: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What acceleration really means**
Think of velocity as telling you how fast and in which direction you are moving. Acceleration tells you how quickly that velocity itself is changing. So it is change divided by time, $$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$ in $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

Step 2: **Write the clean definition**
Because velocity is a vector, any change in speed or direction counts. The full examiner-safe definition is: acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
